title: They Came to Slay - The Queer Culture of DnD
author: Thom James Carter
synopsis:
A fun read, but as many reviews point out it doesn’t have a lot of depth. I’d assume it’s most likely to attract people already invested in queer TTRPGs, but doesn’t offer much new to that audience. I was also surprised that it didn’t touch on other games at all - it’s primarily about D&D which is fair enough, and I wouldn’t usually criticise something for what it isn’t trying to cover, but when you talk about queerness and TTRPGs, all of the exciting stuff has happened away from D&D. The indie community is very queer, and some incredible work has been done in that space, far beyond ‘hey your tiefling can be gay’.

It does also need an edit - some of the language is very online blog style, distractingly so. The history of D&D chapter has some infuriating quirks (“1979 A.D.” etc).

It is enjoyable though, and the author’s joy and love for D&D come through really well, and are infectious.

synopsis: Some great writing and many engaging stories contained within, but it's big and messy and sprawling and not always in a good way.

title: Die, My Love
author: Ariana Harwicz
synopsis: Could not put this down. The writing is fantastic, you're completely drawn into her psyche, and it's a dark place!

title: Why I’m No Longer Talking to White People About Race
cover: covers/book/Why I’m No Longer Talking to White People About Race.jpg
author: Reni Eddo-Lodge
synopsis: Difficult to know what to say, other than it's such a valuable read, especially here in the UK where we tend to see the state of things in the US and build a narrative of 'well things are so much better over here, we just don't have the same issues', completely incorrectly.

title: The Art of Fielding
author: Chad Harbach
synopsis: Great characters and a really warm, fulfilling experience.

title: The Break
author: Pietro Grossi
synopsis: Beautifully written account of a quiet life, a man who finds everything he needs in routine and simple pleasures, and then had to deal with changes forced upon him. Highly recommended.

title: Pereira Maintains
author: Antonio Tabucchi
synopsis: A slight sense of unease in the language as you work through, which keeps you at a distance. Though that mirrors the main character's attempts to remain at a distance from events in his country. By the end though it's a powerful and well earned transformation, with an impactful act closing it out.

title: The Remains of the Day
author: Kazuo Ishiguro
synopsis: Brilliant book, very well narrated by Dominic West. Incredibly unreliable narrator, though he manages to convey more to the reader than he's aware of himself. Just a fantastic study of a restrained, tragic character who is strong and flawed in equal measure. Great ending too, powerful and affecting.

title: A Fraction of the Whole
author: Steve Toltz
synopsis:
I don't generally like books this long, and so I was wary about even starting this, but I've breezed through it and enjoyed every minute, to the extent that it's probably one of my favourite books, and I was quite sad to see it end. Ordinarily I love to see the end of a book, to have it closed off, but this is one of the few where it could have continued almost indefinitely.

I had it described to me (by Mr B's in Bath, best bookshop ever) as a brilliant mess. Obviously a 700 page book probably isn't going to be gold on every single page. But I'd gone in expecting something quite patchy, which wasn't the case. Some parts are stronger than others, but by and large it maintains a consistently high quality throughout. What makes it special are the frequent drops of observational genius that litter it from start to finish.

Every time I read this I would laugh out loud, agree vehemently with something a character thought or said, and come away with an overall warmth. Highly recommend this book to anyone.

title: Signs Preceding the End of the World
cover: covers/book/Signs Preceding the End of the World.jpg
author: Yuri Herrera
synopsis:
Aside from a quick 15 minute initial stint before bed, I read this whole book (short though it is) is one sitting, I just couldn't put it down. It's beautifully written, unsurprisingly not a single moment is wasted in its brief word count. It's a fascinating insight into a young Mexican girl's view of her own world, that of the US she ventures into, and the complicated tangled nature of the relationship between the two.

The translator's note is also well worth reading, giving a glimpse into the, very successful, effort to properly translate the qualities of the original, retaining the very local flavour of the border situation and the book's protagonist. Speaking of which, she's the star of the whole thing, strong and wilful, never merely a passenger in her own adventure, but also endearingly human and vulnerable. With so little space to work with, she's easily one of the most real characters I've had the pleasure of reading about.

title: The Trial
author: Franz Kafka
synopsis: Difficult to come to this one fresh, and I struggled to find something to really latch on to for a long time. By the end though I did really enjoy it, and can see why it's become such a classic.

title: Masters of Doom - How Two Guys Created an Empire and Transformed Pop Culture
cover: covers/book/Masters of Doom - How Two Guys Created an Empire and Transformed Pop Culture.jpg
author: David Kushner
synopsis: Great book, lots of insight into a fascinating story from the early days of gaming. I was around for a lot of it but had no idea about most of the drama.

title: The Dig
author: Cynan Jones
synopsis: I've been putting off writing any notes on this one as I'm not sure I can do it justice. Basically it's one of the best books I've ever read. The writing is incredible, the images and emotions it conjures are visceral and fundamental in a way I don't think I've quite experienced in a book before. It's tense and fantastic and everyone should read it. The only criticism would be a less than fully satisfying ending.

title: Metropole
author: Ferenc Karinthy
synopsis: Brilliant book. The opening few days of his struggle to be understood are incredibly claustrophobic, it was like my worst nightmare come true. Eventually you get a sense of, if not what is actually going on, at least what the book is doing and where it is going. By the end it has painted a really haunting picture of the modern world where people shout at each other constantly without listening, every person living nearly entirely in their own solipsistic world. Despite the age of the book it feels perfectly appropriate in the age of internet outrage and a post-Brexit Britain after a vote that clearly felt more like a cry for attention and a voice than any reasoned judgment on the issue at hand.

title: The Death House
author: Sarah Pinborough
synopsis: Great characters and really strong writing across the entire spectrum of emotion. You don't get much detail, but the world is a fully realised one. Definitely enjoyed this.

title: A Whole Life
author: Robert Seethaler
synopsis: Polished this one off in a day. A very different kind of character to the ones you normally read about, written without any condescension. It's an engaging portrait of one man's life, more eventful than the blurb and reviews suggested, but with a narrow focus that somehow channels significant universality. It's one that is easy to connect with and will stay with you.

title: Fire Season - Field notes from a wilderness lookout
cover: covers/book/Fire Season - Field notes from a wilderness lookout.jpg
author: Philip Connors
synopsis: I guess I'd give it 3.5 really if I could. It was a decent book, I enjoyed it and am glad I read it. However with it following a writer who spends his summers alone on the side of a mountain watching for fires, I expected more ruminations on solitude etc. Those elements are in there, and these sections are my favourite in the book, but they're too few and far between for me. The rest is made up of history of America's response to, and attempts to deal with, forest fires. It's all fascinating stuff, hence still giving it a positive score, just wasn't quite what I was hoping.

title: Billy Lynn’s Long Halftime Walk
author: Ben Fountain
synopsis: Great book, really enjoyed it. Presents our modern western world (specifically America, though I found it broadly applicable to the UK as well) through the eyes of a soldier returning from a traumatic battle in Iraq. As you'd expect it highlights how out of place our priorities are, and just generally provides a great critique. It's nothing new I guess but it was really well done, nicely written, and the characters were interesting and complex, the musings poignant and insightful.

title: Labyrinths - Selected Stories and Other Writings
cover: covers/book/Labyrinths - Selected Stories and Other Writings.jpg
author: Jorge Luis Borges
synopsis:
This was my introduction to Borges, and while some stories work better than others, overall this is consistently some of the best writing I've ever read. It took me over 8 months to finish as I so regularly read one story then have to put the book down to let that one story settle, so thought provoking are they.

It's a very engaging read, and if you like quality writing at all I would recommend it.

title: A Tale for the Time Being
cover: covers/book/A Tale for the Time Being.jpg
author: Ruth Ozeki
synopsis: Took a little while for me to fully get into this, but it's a great book and becomes a real page turner towards the end.

title: Station Eleven
author: Emily St. John Mandel
synopsis: Really enjoyed this one, deserves all the praise it's been getting. Great writing, interesting characters, very moving and thoughtful.

title: Lexicon
author: Max Barry
synopsis: Very enjoyable thriller, though it only just keeps it together in the final act.

title: Strange Bodies
author: Marcel Theroux
synopsis: Great book, it had a similar feel to [b:Boxer, Beetle|7988426|Boxer, Beetle|Ned Beauman|https://d.gr-assets.com/books/1278351360s/7988426.jpg|12455322], which I read recently. The protagonist was utterly compelling, and the framing device lends the whole thing a hint of sadness and inevitability. There's quite a bit early on that seems to be relying on keeping details from the reader as though it is a mystery, when what is going on is broadly very easy to figure out. Doesn't hurt it much though, I still thoroughly enjoyed it.

title: Silently and Very Fast
author: Catherynne M. Valente
synopsis: Gorgeous writing and a really original book. It somehow manages to make the concept of AI feel fresh, which much fiction fails to do. Well worth reading, and even possibly re-reading and analysing piece by piece.

title: 2001 - A Space Odyssey
author: Arthur C. Clarke
synopsis: Difficult to avoid comparisons to the film obviously, and I think it comes out on the losing side every time. ACC isn't the most literary writer anyway, but The City and the Stars was leagues ahead of this for quality of writing. It's odd but it almost feels like a novelisation of a film, in that it basically just seems to be the film but with extra bits added in to pad out the length, but they don't add much to the experience.

title: What I Talk About When I Talk About Running
cover: covers/book/What I Talk About When I Talk About Running.jpg
author: Haruki Murakami, Haruki Murakami
synopsis: I haven't read any of his fiction work (yet), but being a runner this intrigued me so I picked up the audiobook. I thought it was great, there's a lot of wisdom in here, as well as humour. It comes across as a very personal book, unsurprisingly, but it's a valuable read especially for fellow runners.

title: Polystom
author: Adam Roberts
synopsis: Enjoyed this, and like Stone, the other Roberts book I've read, it had an interestingly unlikeable protagonist. It just didn't feel as strong as Stone, and I doubt it will have a lasting impact on me.

title: A Calculated Life
author: Anne Charnock
synopsis: Really good debut novel, a thoughtful look at a well trodden sci fi concept. Great world building without any excess space specifically given over to it. As with all good literature, it communicates larger ideas through small moments.

title: Galapagos
author: Kurt Vonnegut
synopsis: It was decent, but felt like the ideas driving it held enough for a short story rather than a 300+ page novel.

title: Room
author: Emma Donoghue
synopsis: Really enjoyed this. Though the premise is obviously quite dark, the choice to have the child as the narrator, who doesn't realise that his life should not have been as it was, gives it a certain levity and charm.

title: The Inverted World
author: Christopher Priest
synopsis: Well written and enjoyable, but the twist wasn't as much of a gut punch as I'd heard.

title: Under the Skin
author: Michel Faber
synopsis: The very rare situation where the film is better than the book. They're also barely related at all, so the comparison perhaps isn't fair. The book is decent enough, but it isn't subtle with its meat-is-murder message, there's plenty of gaping plot holes (and these things don't usually trouble me too much), and by now everyone knows what genre it is and the basic premise, so the slow reveal doesn't really have any impact.

title: A Time of Gifts - On Foot to Constantinople - From the Hook of Holland to the Middle Danube
cover: covers/book/A Time of Gifts - On Foot to Constantinople - From the Hook of Holland to the Middle Danube.jpg
author: Patrick Leigh Fermor
synopsis:
Simultaneously charming and utterly irritating. It describes a journey that you feel just couldn't happen in modern day Europe. Though as pronounced as the time gap is, the class gap creates even more distance, certainly for me. There are odd hints at a self awareness of this, but most of the book suggests otherwise. Parts of it are fascinating, but he has a tendency to go on huge tangents that aren't necessarily to do with his actual experiences.

Last note, I listened to the audiobook and the narration is absolutely spot on, exactly the voice that you would expect.

title: Boxer, Beetle
author: Ned Beauman
synopsis: Really entertaining and well written.

title: Double Star
author: Robert A. Heinlein
synopsis: The first Heinlein book I've read, and honestly it is quite dated. I had some fun with it, but the same concept in better hands could have yielded something far more interesting.

title: The Road
author: Cormac McCarthy
synopsis: A really mesmerising read. It's simultaneously very tense and just as melancholic. Love the prose and the style, and just overall can't recommend it enough.

title: Cargo Fever
author: Will Buckingham
synopsis: A very funny and exciting adventure!

title: Foundation
author: Isaac Asimov
synopsis: This has lost a little of its impact since I read it as a youngster, now that I see the unlikely nature of the psychohistory Asimov describes. It does also rob the story of some tension when the key scenes mostly involve people knowing when not to act. That same interplay between the sweeping, large scale development and the individual conflicts is what makes it supremely interesting though.

title: The Flame Alphabet
author: Ben Marcus
synopsis: I can't really not give this a five, especially since its average rating is such a poor indication of its quality. From the concept - language has become toxic to adults - I expected a fun, clever novel that plays with words. Instead it took me by surprise by being dark, oppressive, fiercely intelligent and, most of all, disturbingly surreal. Text becomes painful to adults in the book, and the book itself is almost painful at times. I'm not sure how he managed it, but it's a very powerful experience, and not always enjoyable in a traditional sense, so I can see why it has attracted a lot of negative reviews. Still, if you can cope with experimental literature that doesn't follow the normal rules, I would highly recommend it.

title: High-Rise
author: J.G. Ballard
synopsis: Very clever, dark satire and take down of modern society.That isn't something you can't see in a million other places, but the technology aspect (in the broadest sense of the term, including the architecture etc) was uniquely interesting. I really enjoyed it, though I'm not convinced with the treatment of gender.

title: The Martian
author: Andy Weir
synopsis: I was all set to think that this was probably not worth the hype, but it was a lot of fun and a really tense, gripping story. As I see mentioned regularly, the main character is great, and for once I'm actually looking forward to a movie version since this story is just made for it. It's not 'literature' in a high brow sense of the word, but that's fine -  the writing is good, which was my worry going in.

title: The Human Division
author: John Scalzi
synopsis: There is, at best, a three star book in here somewhere, but it's unfortunately buried amongst a hefty amount of unengaging, pointless story telling. Much like Zoe's Tale it comes together a bit more in the final quarter, and the last of the two bonus pieces is sweet, but it would have been much more palatable edited into a single narrative with the fat trimmed off. Even then it would have been nothing more than an enjoyable attempt to keep the wheels turning on the Old Man's War series.

title: The Demolished Man
author: Alfred Bester
synopsis: Gripping, loved the struggle between Reich and Powell, and it finished unexpectedly strong.

title: The War of the Worlds
author: H.G. Wells
synopsis: It has a similar, dated language style to The Time Machine, but I think has not fared as well as that book. Here it relies too much on the novelty of the subject matter, where The Time Machine stands up more as an interesting story on its own, the two sides of future humans being more complex and interesting than the Martians here. Still, it was interesting and, keeping the context and age in mind, impressive.

title: The Catcher in the Rye
author: J.D. Salinger
synopsis: What a great, tragic character. I think the people painting him as a whiner are kind of missing it.

title: Complete Stories and Poems of Edgar Allan Poe
cover: covers/book/Complete Stories and Poems of Edgar Allan Poe.jpg
author: Edgar Allan Poe

title: Zoe’s Tale
author: John Scalzi
synopsis: The other reviews are right in that the book comes together in the final third. Before that I'd been expecting to give it two stars. Part of the problem I think was the audio book format. The narrator's performance is a little too convincing for the teenagers, especially as they make absolutely ridiculous decisions (Roanoke's native predators for example) and spout general teenage-drama nonsense. In the end I did enjoy it as a fan of the series, and I definitely warmed to Zoe, but it's the weakest book by far, and I'm hoping for more from The Human Division.

title: Nod
author: Adrian Barnes
synopsis: Could not put this down, really well written, very dark and twisted.

title: The Time Machine
author: H.G. Wells
synopsis: Fascinating, enjoyable read.

title: Self-Reference Engine
author: Toh EnJoe
synopsis: A fascinating read. It's definitely a single narrative despite the common propensity to compare it to a collection of short stories, it's just not a simple, linear narrative. Essentially it takes a bunch of difficult ideas such as altering the past and forgoes the usual arbitrary rules and omissions that writers make so that they can tell a single, clear story.

title: Flatland - A Romance of Many Dimensions
cover: covers/book/Flatland - A Romance of Many Dimensions.jpg
author: Edwin A. Abbott
synopsis: Fun and intriguing thought experiment, the satire was unexpected and very clever, as good as any 20th century equivalent I've read.

title: Infinity Welcomes Careful Drivers
author: Grant Naylor
synopsis: Chris Barrie's narration is brilliant, but the book is mostly a rehash of the early episodes, so most of the funny bits are just lifted directly from the show.

title: The Particle at the End of the Universe - How the Hunt for the Higgs Boson Leads Us to the Edge of a New World
cover: covers/book/The Particle at the End of the Universe - How the Hunt for the Higgs Boson Leads Us to the Edge of a New World.jpg
author: Sean Carroll
synopsis: Really nice balance between the science and the stories behind the science.

title: The Infinite Book - A Short Guide to the Boundless, Timeless and Endless
cover: covers/book/The Infinite Book - A Short Guide to the Boundless, Timeless and Endless.jpg
author: John D. Barrow

title: Born to Run - A Hidden Tribe, Superathletes, and the Greatest Race the World Has Never Seen
cover: covers/book/Born to Run - A Hidden Tribe, Superathletes, and the Greatest Race the World Has Never Seen.jpg
author: Christopher McDougall

title: The Sagan Diary
author: John Scalzi
synopsis: Beautifully written and thoughtful discussion of important themes within the Old Man's War series and life more generally. I think the negative reviews are from those expecting similar style and content to the other books, but there is no action here, and no plot to speak of. I very much enjoyed it though, and would argue that it is the best writing I've seen from Scalzi.

title: The Unbearable Lightness of Being a Prawn Cracker
cover: covers/book/The Unbearable Lightness of Being a Prawn Cracker.jpg
author: Will Self
synopsis: Good fun.

title: Ready Player One
author: Ernest Cline
synopsis: Complete self indulgence for geeks, it's brilliant. I listened to the audio book narrated by Wil Wheaton, which I would particularly recommend, especially since it just makes the whole thing even geekier.

title: The Lighthouse
author: Alison Moore
synopsis: I really loved this book. The anxiety driven psychological issues endured by pretty much every character are powerfully depicted, and intertwine beautifully, even while they differ. Some quote on the front describes it as "melancholy and haunting", and they are exactly right. The repetition of certain scenes and themes worked for me, and though the symbolism is a little in your face, the key events are often inferred rather than described directly, which allows the book to retain that "haunting" atmosphere. You do root for Futh and feel anger towards those doing him harm, even though he is an absolute waste of space, because he is that way for a reason. He's certainly a character that will stay with me, and to have a lasting impact is all you really want from a book.

title: The Hundred-Year-Old Man Who Climbed Out of the Window and Disappeared
cover: covers/book/The Hundred-Year-Old Man Who Climbed Out of the Window and Disappeared.jpg
author: Jonas Jonasson

title: The Zombie Survival Guide - Complete Protection from the Living Dead
cover: covers/book/The Zombie Survival Guide - Complete Protection from the Living Dead.jpg
author: Max Brooks
synopsis: It's a brilliant idea, except at some point you realise you're reading a how to book for a situation that will never arise, and it feels kind of pointless.

title: Fantastic Four - Inhumans
author: José Ladrönn, Carlos Pacheco, Karl Kesel, Mark Bagley, Jorge Lucas, Rafael Marín

title: Monoculture - How One Story is Changing Everything
cover: covers/book/Monoculture - How One Story is Changing Everything.jpg
author: F.S. Michaels

title: Batman - A Death in the Family
cover: covers/book/Batman - A Death in the Family.jpg
author: Jim Starlin

title: Batman - Arkham Asylum - A Serious House on Serious Earth
cover: covers/book/Batman - Arkham Asylum - A Serious House on Serious Earth.jpg
author: Grant Morrison

title: Batman, Volume 1 - The Court of Owls
cover: covers/book/Batman, Volume 1 - The Court of Owls.jpg
author: Scott Snyder

title: Batman, Volume 2 - The City of Owls
cover: covers/book/Batman, Volume 2 - The City of Owls.jpg

title: Snow Crash
author: Neal Stephenson
synopsis:
Decided to give up on this one, I'm over half-way through but can't bring myself to go back to it. Turns out audiobook was a bad format for this - the narrator grates and even at 2x the constant descriptions and diversions and info dumps take too long, whereas I could have skim read certain sections in written form.

That being said, I'm not sure which bits I wouldn't have been skim reading. I just didn't find it very compelling at all, most of the information is unnecessary, the world he's built feels way too ridiculous and out of touch with reality, and it all ends up being very boring. I bought Anathem a long time ago on Kindle and though I was looking forward to reading it, I was hesitant to commit to such a large book, having tried this I'm not sure I will ever get round to it.

Overall this was just really disappointing.

title: The Reality Dysfunction
author: Peter F. Hamilton
synopsis:
I only made it 250 pages through. But some of my favourite books have managed to stir the full range of emotions through a dramatic story populated with engaging characters in 250 pages. So far this is a series of mostly humdrum events, with unlikeable characters and mediocre writing.

I don't mind long books sometimes. I loved The Book of the New Sun for example, but this is definitely not on Gene Wolf's level. And to think it is the first of a three parter? Eventually the realisation of the time required versus the (lack of) enjoyment I was receiving got to be too much, and I gave up.
